To identify the distinctive features of Arab thought in its broadest sense.
Our method here begins from two principles.
The first is that we are talking about characteristics acquired through history.

Our approach does not allow us to speak of innate racial characteristics that make the thought of one people fundamentally different from that of another people or another human “race.” To do so would lead us into racism or racial chauvinism.

When we say that Arab thought has distinctive characteristics, we mean that it acquired certain features during its historical development, from the closing period of the Jāhiliyya and the beginnings of Islam down to the end of the Middle Ages.

These features were the historical result of a long series of changes in the kinds of questions that the development of Arab-Islamic society placed before Arab thought. Thought had to deal with those questions and search for answers to them. The methods it used, and the level it reached, developed alongside the growth of scientific knowledge about nature and the world as a whole.

The objective forces that produced these characteristics worked through the internal mechanisms of Arab thought itself. But those mechanisms could not have operated in isolation from the general laws governing the development of human thought, which are themselves objectively connected with the general laws governing the development of human society.
The internal laws governing the thought of a particular people are one concrete way in which those general laws take effect.
This is the basis on which, throughout this book, we identify the characteristics of Arab thought as they emerged and developed from simpler forms into more complex ones.

The second principle concerns the development of Arab-Islamic philosophy in particular, and the relationship between the features specific to its development and the general features found in the development of philosophical thought as a whole, regardless of place and time.
We accept without argument the historical fact that Arab-Islamic philosophy followed a particular path of development. This gave it a distinctive character.
On the one hand, its development was tied to the development of Islamic religious thought. On the other, it absorbed elements of both the Greek and Eastern philosophical traditions.

But this does not mean that we can accept Hegel’s claim that Eastern philosophy as a whole existed within a separate and self-contained framework, cut off from the general history of philosophy outside that framework and from the common features of philosophical development.
A comprehensive and realistic view shows that this claim is wrong.

Every philosophy develops under its own particular conditions, but no philosophy falls outside the historical forces that shape the general development of philosophical thought across different times and places.
By these historical forces, we mean the following:
Every philosophy develops through a struggle between materialism and idealism.
It also develops through a struggle between dialectical thought and metaphysics understood as a static way of thinking.
The character and level of a philosophy are connected with the character and historical level reached by scientific knowledge of nature.
Major qualitative changes in philosophy often come before social and political upheavals. At a particular historical moment, those philosophical changes become a theoretical basis for such upheavals.

Philosophy can appear only through categories and concepts. Philosophy is the most abstract of the forms of social consciousness, and philosophical abstraction can only be expressed through the language of categories and concepts, whereas art expresses itself through images.

If we look at Arab-Islamic philosophy both through its own particular history and through these general features shared by philosophy as a whole, we can understand the relationship between the two as a dialectical relationship between the particular and the general.

Something does not stop sharing common features with other things simply because it has its own distinctive character. Those common features appear within its particular form and are realized through it.
The same is true of Arab-Islamic philosophy. The distinctive path of its own development does not separate it from the common features found in the development of philosophy more generally.
We do not say this simply as an abstract theoretical claim.

We say it because this is what we see when we follow Arab-Islamic philosophy through its actual historical movement and through the conflicts it was forced to undergo: conflicts within itself, and conflicts with opponents who defended the ideology of the dominant social order.

Modern idealist and bourgeois researchers have used Hegel’s idea of a separate and self-contained Eastern philosophy and applied it to Arab-Islamic philosophy. They have used this idea of “particularity” to remove Arab-Islamic philosophy from the wider history of the philosophical struggle between materialism and idealism.

The disagreement over the relationship between the “particular character” of our philosophical heritage and the general features shared by the development of philosophy throughout the world is therefore not simply a methodological or academic disagreement.
At its core, it is an ideological disagreement.
What, then, is the identity of the philosophical heritage we are proposing to study?
There is no doubt that it has its own historical “particularity,” although, as we have seen, there is disagreement over how far that particularity goes.

Does it form a closed world, cut off from the general course of philosophical history? Or does it stand in relation to philosophy as the particular stands to the general—forming part of that wider history and sharing the common features found in philosophy everywhere and in every age?
But to whom, or to what, does this “particularity” actually belong, in real historical and objective terms?
Is this philosophy an Arab product, so that we should call it Arab philosophy? Or is it an Islamic product created by people from many different peoples, so that we should call it Islamic philosophy?
And what exactly does it mean to say that it is Arab or Islamic?

Does it mean that its creators were Arabs of pure blood and descent? Does it mean that Muslims from many different peoples took part in producing it? Or does the question go beyond national or ethnic origin altogether and concern an intellectual and linguistic identity instead?
In other words, should the identity of this philosophy be determined by the content of its thought and by the language through which that thought was expressed?
In its general form, this question has been debated since modern scholars first began to study the heritage.
Earlier Arab writers, however, do not seem to have regarded it as a problem at all. We do not find them giving any particular name to the philosophy of the heritage itself.
This suggests that they saw no barrier separating it from the general history of philosophy as they knew it.

That view seems to have remained dominant down to the time of Ibn Khaldūn. He expressed it very clearly when he wrote that the rational sciences are natural to human beings because human beings are thinking creatures. They belong to no particular religion. People of every religion can study them and are equal in their ability to understand and investigate them. They have existed among humanity since civilization first appeared, and they are known as the sciences of philosophy and wisdom.
What we do find among earlier writers are certain names for the philosophers themselves.
They sometimes call them the “philosophers of Islam.” Al-Ghazālī calls them “those who philosophize within Islam.” Ibn Khaldūn calls them “the speculative thinkers among the people of Islam.”
But these names do not tell us the identity of their philosophy. They tell us only that these individuals belonged to the society that had formed under the banner of Islam.
They do not mean that their philosophy represented the Islamic faith.

If they did, Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq could not have understood the phrase “philosophers of Islam” to mean that “those who practiced philosophy under Islam, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, are called the philosophers of Islam.” Nor would he have had to admit that their philosophy is called Islamic philosophy only “in the conventional sense,” rather than in a religious sense—even though he himself was keen to use the phrase in support of calling it Islamic philosophy in that latter sense.
We find the same thing when earlier historians call al-Kindī at one moment “the philosopher of the Arabs” and at another “the philosopher of Islam.”
They did not mean that al-Kindī had created an “Arab philosophy” or an “Islamic philosophy” in the sense of racial or religious identity.

What they meant is captured by the judge Ṣāʿid when he wrote that “there was no one in Islam”—by which he meant the Islamic lands—“who became famous for the sciences of philosophy and was called a philosopher other than Yaʿqūb,” meaning al-Kindī.
So the works of the earlier writers do not give us a defined “identity” for the philosophical heritage.
Modern Orientalists and Arab scholars, by contrast, have debated the question at length, and the disagreement remains unresolved.
But their debate has focused on only one side of the problem: the “nationality” of this philosophy, if we may call it that.
They have tried to decide whether it belongs to the Arab “race” or to several different human “races” within the state of the Caliphate.
They have not tried to establish its identity through the intellectual content of the philosophy itself and through the relationship between that content and social reality.
Two positions have therefore emerged, and both are one-sided.
One calls it “Arab philosophy” because it was written in Arabic.
The other calls it “Islamic philosophy” because most of its leading figures were not of Arab origin.
Each position takes one of these two facts and ignores the other, almost as though the second fact did not exist or had no importance.

The disagreement also makes the problem look superficial. On one side, it becomes a formal question about language. On the other, it becomes a question about whether the philosophers belonged to one ethnic origin or another.
But the issue goes much deeper than that.

The important point is not simply that this philosophy was written in Arabic, considered only as the outward language or vocabulary in which it appeared. Nor is the important point simply whether most of its leading figures were Arabs or non-Arabs, understood in this narrow and superficial ethnic sense.
We need to look at two deeper facts together.
First, the philosophy of this heritage was written in Arabic and no other language.

Second, the people who produced and represented it came from several different peoples, with several different languages. During the Middle Ages, these peoples became part of a shared state—or a succession of shared states—connected with Islam not only as a religion but, above all, as a historical reality: Islam had become the name of a particular historical social order.
A scientific approach therefore requires us, first, to take both facts seriously and, second, to search for the deeper reality that lies not in either fact by itself but in the unity of the two.
We must begin by looking at the place of the Arabic language within our intellectual heritage as a whole. From there, we can understand its particular place within the philosophical heritage.
Language, as such, is a means through which social consciousness is expressed within a particular historical society.
In this sense, language is a social instrument.

It is true that a language takes shape, grows, and develops through internal mechanisms and laws of its own. These have a greater degree of independence than the actual content of the thought the language expresses.
But this does not mean that the internal laws of language operate in isolation from the movement of thought or from the movement of society, both of which language serves to express.

Language is historical. It does not arise, grow, and develop outside the history of a particular form of social consciousness. And that social consciousness, in turn, does not arise, grow, or develop outside the history of the society to which it belongs.

From the rise of Islam to the point when the social and political order of the Caliphate had taken a settled form, Arabic-speaking society was absorbing enormous economic, social, and demographic changes.
Arabic itself necessarily had to absorb those changes—in its vocabulary and in its philological structure—through its own internal processes, which also had a history of their own.

Seen from this angle, Arabic was using all its resources of word formation and expression to create a new vocabulary capable of carrying the ideas produced by the structure of Arab-Islamic social relations during the Middle Ages.

Its own internal processes—derivation, the formation of new words, Arabization, and so on—proved flexible enough to absorb the different forms of social consciousness that belonged to this new structure.
We can therefore say that the Arabic vocabulary and grammatical system inherited from the Jāhiliyya were not the same Arabic that later carried the intellectual and philosophical heritage down to us.
The earlier language had a simpler structure, closely connected with the simpler history of Arab tribal society.
The later language had a much more complex structure, just as Arab-Islamic society itself had acquired a much more complex history.
That complexity existed on several levels at once. Economic and social forces, politics, culture, and demographic change all became intertwined and interacted with one another.

We stress the demographic element because this human mixture played an enormously important historical role in the development of relations of production, with the distinctive forms they took in that period. It also played a major role in shaping the intellectual heritage that expressed the social structure created by those relations.
The Arab-Islamic world brought together the human energies of many peoples in one historical experience. They interacted through social activity and through the production of knowledge.
This gave new features to their shared material and intellectual activity—to the work of both material and intellectual productive forces.

Those features appeared both in social relations and in individual work. And within this particular historical setting, they were also expressed through a shared language that absorbed the results of the entire experience with an almost extraordinary power.

Its vocabulary, its word structures, its grammar, and its forms of expression came to embody a whole network of relationships produced by this turbulent historical interaction, with all its varied and complex contradictions.
At the intellectual level, philosophical thought in particular provided a framework in which those contradictions could come together.

This was because philosophy, more than any other form of social consciousness, directly confronts the great problems of the universe, society, and thought. And it does so from positions that cannot remain neutral toward the contradictions and struggles taking place in the world outside the mind.
